title: Psalm 45: A Song for the King's Wedding
summary: A court poet sings in honor of the king on his wedding day. He praises the king's beauty, his gracious speech, and his victories on behalf of truth, humility, and justice, and then addresses him with the words "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever." The second half turns to the royal bride, urging her to leave her father's house for the king, describes her procession into the palace, and promises the king sons and lasting fame.
story: Psalm 45 is the only wedding song in the Psalter, and one of its royal psalms, poems centered on the king descended from David. It follows the national lament of Psalm 44, and its placement suggests that the answer to Israel's defeats lies in God's king, the one who rides out for truth and justice. Like the other royal psalms, it was preserved long after Israel had any king, because readers came to hear in it a promise about the king God would one day send. It stands at the head of a sequence that moves toward God's reign over the nations in Psalms 46 to 48.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to the sons of Korah, calls it a Maskil and "a love song", and sets it to a tune called "The Lilies", whose melody is unknown. The poet speaks of himself in verse 1 as a skillful writer reciting his verses to the king, which suggests a professional court singer.

Which king is not stated. Solomon has been a common suggestion because of his many foreign marriages, including the daughter of Pharaoh, and his wealth. Some have proposed Ahab, who married Jezebel, a Phoenician princess from Sidon (1 Kings 16:31), because of the reference to Tyre, another Phoenician city, and because 1 Kings 22:39 mentions an ivory house Ahab built; others doubt a Judean collection would preserve a song for a northern king remembered so poorly. Still others think the psalm was composed for use at more than one royal wedding. The mention of Ophir, a distant source of fine gold (1 Kings 9:28), and of ivory palaces points to the prosperous monarchy period, but the text itself does not let us name the occasion.
cultural:
Royal weddings in the ancient world were affairs of state. They sealed alliances between kingdoms, and foreign princesses brought their households and wealth with them. The call to the bride to "Forget your people and your father's house" (verse 10) reflects the reality that she would leave her homeland for good and join her husband's people. The gifts from the Daughter of Tyre (a poetic way of naming the city of Tyre, a wealthy Phoenician trading port) show foreign powers seeking favor with the new queen.

The king's garments are scented with myrrh, aloes, and cassia, expensive imported spices, and the court musicians play from palaces decorated with ivory. Carved ivory inlays have been excavated at Samaria and elsewhere in the region, and the prophet Amos condemns houses of ivory (Amos 3:15). Anointing with oil marked a king's installation, and the "oil of joy" in verse 7 links that anointing with the gladness of a feast. The queen at the king's right hand stands in the place of honor.
literary: The psalm has a clear frame: the poet's introduction (verse 1) and his closing promise (verses 16 to 17). Between them are two panels. Verses 2 to 9 address the king, moving from his appearance and speech to his warfare, his throne, and his wedding garments. Verses 10 to 15 address the bride and describe her procession. The whole is courtly praise, using the exaggerated language of royal poetry found across the ancient Near East. The most debated line is verse 6, where the king himself appears to be addressed as God, followed at once by the distinction "God, your God, has anointed you" in verse 7.

outline.t: The king's beauty, grace, and victories
His throne, his anointing, and his court
The bride's procession to the palace
Sons for the king and lasting praise

doctrines.note: The psalm's language about the king outruns any actual king of Judah. His throne endures forever, his reign is marked by justice, and he is anointed above his companions. Jewish and Christian readers came to hear in it the promised anointed king.

The king's rule is defined by what it serves: truth, humility, and justice (verse 4), and a scepter of justice (verse 6). The psalm pictures kingship as righteousness put to work, the pattern of God's own reign.
Marriage is celebrated here with joy, beauty, and public honor. The bride's leaving of her father's house echoes Genesis 2:24, where a man leaves father and mother and holds fast to his wife.

words.note: Mashach, to anoint. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah (and, through Greek, Christ). Kings and priests were anointed with oil. In verse 7 God anoints the king "above your companions", marking him out from all others.

Kisse, throne. The throne stands for the king's rule. God promised David that his throne would be established forever (2 Samuel 7:16), and verse 6 echoes that promise, whatever one decides about how to translate the line.

Anvah, humility or meekness. It is striking in a war song: the king rides out on behalf of truth, humility, and justice. The word is rare, and it colors this king's power with a quality kings usually lacked.

christ: Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes verses 6 and 7 as God's words to the Son, to show that the Son is greater than the angels: his throne is forever, and he has been anointed above his companions. The writer reads the psalm's address "O God" as fitting Jesus fully, while "God, your God" distinguishes him from the Father, which the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity. The wedding theme also runs toward Christ. The prophets pictured God as Israel's husband, the New Testament calls the church the bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25-32), and Revelation ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb. Christians have read Psalm 45 as a royal wedding song that finds its fullest meaning in that marriage.

hard.q: How should verse 6 be translated? Is a human king really called God?
hard.a: The Hebrew most naturally reads "Your throne, O God", addressing the king. Some scholars think this is court hyperbole: the Davidic king was God's representative and adopted son (Psalm 2:7), and the word elohim is occasionally used of human judges or leaders (Exodus 21:6 is often cited). Others translate differently, for example as a statement that the throne is God's, or as a reference to a divine throne, to avoid calling the king God, though these readings are grammatically harder. The ancient Greek translation read it as an address to God, and Hebrews follows that. Christians have seen here a line that only makes full sense of a king who is both God and anointed by God. Readers can hold that conviction while acknowledging that the original singer may have meant something more modest, which the later story filled out.

questions: The king rides out for truth, humility, and justice. Which of those three do you most expect from leaders, and which do you least expect?
The bride is called to leave her father's house. What does it cost to belong fully to someone, whether in marriage or in faith?
Hebrews applies this psalm to Jesus. What does it add to your picture of Christ to imagine him as a bridegroom king?
